Chapter 1. Wondering About the World—Myths, Curiosity, and the Search for Truth.
You know, it usually starts with a simple question. Picture a kid lying in the grass, staring up at the sky and just wondering—why does the sun move across it? Or maybe someone gets caught in a sudden rainstorm and finds themselves asking, where does thunder actually come from? That spark of curiosity is as old as humanity itself.
For most of our history, people tried to make sense of the world with whatever they had: stories, legends, and the wisdom passed down from elders. The world felt mysterious—sometimes even scary, and always full of questions.
Imagine a small village at dusk. Folks gather around a fire, and the oldest among them starts telling a story—maybe about how the mountains were formed. Not with rocks and time, but with the footsteps of giants. The kids listen, totally captivated, as the tale unfolds. To them, the world is alive with magic. Every river and tree seems to have been shaped by the hands of gods or spirits. These stories comfort us, they entertain, and they help explain the unexplainable.
But with time, people start to notice little cracks in these tales. Maybe a young person wonders, if the sun is being carried by a chariot, why doesn’t it ever fall from the sky? Or, why does the rainbow always show up after it rains, no matter what the elders say about it being a bridge for spirits? The stories are beautiful, but sometimes, they just don’t match what’s actually seen and felt.
That’s when a new kind of magic begins to take root—the magic of asking questions and looking for answers you can actually test and share. Instead of relying only on stories, some folks start searching for patterns, experimenting, observing. They notice the sun rises and sets in a predictable way. Rainbows appear only when sunlight passes through raindrops. The world stays wondrous—but now, it seems to follow rules we can discover for ourselves.
The journey from myth to understanding isn’t about losing our sense of wonder. Actually, it’s just the opposite. The more we learn about how things truly work, the more breathtaking the world becomes. Think about it—the rainbow, once thought to be a supernatural sign, turns out to be a dance of light and water, more intricate and beautiful than any old legend. And those mountains? Instead of the work of giants, they’re shaped by forces deep inside the Earth, moving ever so slowly over millions of years.
Most of us, at some point, feel the pull of both kinds of magic—the comfort of stories, and the excitement of discovery. But the real magic? It’s in the search for what’s true. It’s in being willing to ask, to doubt, to look for evidence. That kind of magic doesn’t fade like stories—it only grows stronger with every new question we ask.
As the fire dies down and the stars appear, the world feels familiar yet strangely new. Stories still have their place, but now there’s a different story unfolding—one written by every single person who’s ever wondered, tested, and learned. This is the magic of reality. And it’s open to anyone, as long as you’re willing to look.
